# **October CPI: Core Inflation Rises Again, Fueling Rate Hike Expectations**


**The**[October Consumer Price Index Report](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm) **rose 0.4% from September, a slower pace than September’s 0.6% jump.** A slower pace still means prices are rising, just less quickly. Because BLS did not collect data in October 2025 during the government shutdown, there is no year-over-year comparison for headline CPI this month.


**Inflation cooled in October, but cooler isn’t cheaper. Households are still paying more for gas, groceries, and rent, and employers are still absorbing higher costs. Until that pressure lets up, hiring and job switching may go back to being stuck in neutral.**


### **Why prices are staying high**


Gasoline is still the main pressure point. It rose 1.0% in October after a 9.1% surge in September, and it is up 37.4% from a year ago. Energy costs also ripple outward. Transportation services rose 0.8%, motor vehicle insurance rose 0.7%, and food prices rose 0.5%, with groceries up 0.4% and restaurant meals up 0.5%. **Excluding food and energy, prices rose 0.3% for the third straight month, a sign that inflation is holding at an elevated pace.**


### **Why it challenges the Fed**


**Shelter rose 0.3% in October and accounted for over 30% of the monthly increase, with owners’ equivalent rent up 0.3% and rent up 0.2%.** Mortgage rates are still elevated, which keeps would-be buyers in the rental market and drives up overall housing costs. That makes it harder for the Fed to ease up, as higher inflation puts upward pressure on mortgage rates, which then factors into more higher inflation. The October data is fueling expectations of a rate hike in December, possibly a 50 basis point move.


### **What it means for consumers and businesses**


Households are paying more for fuel, food, housing, and insurance, which leaves little room in budgets. Businesses face higher transportation and input costs while customers get more selective, so neither side can easily absorb the pressure. Used car prices, down 1.2% on the month, were one of the few bright spots.


### **What it means for the labor market**


This is shaping up to be a higher-for-longer inflation story, and that is a risk for hiring and worker mobility. Recent BLS reports showed some early signs of life for both employers and workers, but the labor market has been quick to react to shifts in the broader economy. Persistent inflation, a more likely rate hike, and stubborn housing costs could be enough to pull job growth and quits back down in November’s data. Next month’s CPI, due December 10, should offer a clearer read on year-over-year changes and the road ahead.
